event.name: Earthquake Venezuela June 2026
event.documents: JRC documents: GEER report, JRC health security note, ECHO Flash

overview.title: Event overview
overview.content: On 24 June 2026, two major earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela within about 30 seconds of one another: an M7.2 event at 18:04:31 local time (22:04:31 UTC) with epicentre approximately 21 km ENE of San Felipe, Yaracuy State (10.371, -68.556), at a hypocentral depth of 10 km (USGS), and an M7.5 event about one minute later with epicentre offshore/near Catia La Mar, La Guaira State (10.622, -67.194), also at 10 km depth (USGS/GEER). The sequence affected at least seven states, with La Guaira and the Greater Caracas area most severely impacted, and occurred within the Caribbean-South America transpressional plate-boundary zone along the Boconó-San Sebastián-El Pilar fault system. USGS PAGER estimated that, combined, approximately 37,000 people were exposed to violent shaking, 347,000 to severe shaking, 627,000 to very strong shaking and almost 7 million to strong shaking.

hazards.title: Hazard and cascading hazards
hazards.content: The primary hazard was the strike-slip earthquake doublet (M7.2 and M7.5), followed by an intense aftershock sequence: ECHO Flash reported several M4.9-5.2 aftershocks on 29 June, a further M4.2 aftershock on 29 June near Caraballeda, and GEER/ECHO note over 1,000 aftershocks recorded by 7 July. Cascading hazards included widespread liquefaction along the La Guaira coast (68 lateral-spreading/liquefaction features inventoried by GEER, concentrated in La Guaira), over 650 landslides across the Cordillera de la Costa identified from satellite imagery, and localized debris-flow remobilization risk in watersheds historically affected by the 1999 and 2005 events. Industrial/infrastructure cascading effects included an oil leak at the El Palito Refinery and damage with a storage-tank leak at the Morón Petrochemical Complex. Health-security documents also flag an outbreak risk (measles, diphtheria, pertussis, yellow fever, dengue, chikungunya, Zika, Oropouche, malaria) among displaced and overcrowded populations following the earthquakes.

exposure_vulnerability.title: Exposure and vulnerability
exposure_vulnerability.content: The earthquakes struck a densely populated corridor including Caracas (population about 5.5 million) and the coastal La Guaira communities, within 250 km of Venezuela's most populated areas including Valencia and Maracay. USGS PAGER noted that the population in the region resides primarily in vulnerable structures, predominantly unreinforced masonry and adobe buildings. GEER documents geological vulnerability from thick, unconsolidated Quaternary alluvial, lacustrine and debris-flow deposits in La Guaira and the Caracas Valley, which amplify shaking and are liquefaction-prone. The JRC health security note stresses that Venezuela entered the crisis with pre-existing chronic health-system fragility, re-emergence of vaccine-preventable diseases (measles, diphtheria) since the mid-2010s, and millions already facing difficulties accessing health care, safe water and food (PAHO/WHO, 10 July 2026), compounding the earthquake's health impacts.

impacts.title: Impacts
impacts.content: Fatality figures evolved substantially over time and differ by source: ECHO Flash/AVN/UN OCHA reported 32 deaths on 25 June, 235 by 26 June, 1,450 by 29 June, 1,719 by 30 June, 1,943 by 1 July, 2,295 by 2 July, 2,595 by 3 July, 2,954 by 4 July (reported 6 July), 3,535 by 7 July, 3,685 by 8 July, 3,889 by 10 July, and 5,278 by 20 July (per UN OCHA report dated 20 July). The Venezuelan government later released a figure of over 6,000 deaths and nearly 61,000 injured as of 3 August 2026 (Reuters, cited in GEER). Displacement figures also rose over time: ECHO Flash reported 12,700 displaced by 29 June, growing to 17,907 by 20 July, with 1.3 million people affected countrywide and 23,587 people in 107 transitional shelters (41 Caracas, 28 Miranda, 28 La Guaira, 10 Aragua) as of 20 July. Buildings affected rose from 250 (26 June) to 774 (29 June, 189 collapsed) to 856 damaged/190 collapsed by 20 July; 38 hospitals and 433 schools were reported damaged. Economic loss estimates vary: GEM Foundation (ERCC) estimated USD 4.1-7.9 billion across scenarios (25 June-6 July analyses), while the World Bank GRADE methodology estimated USD 19.6 billion in direct physical damage (cited in GEER, August 2026); USGS PAGER's initial red alert suggested losses of 5-20% of Venezuela's GDP. Lifelines were disrupted: 10 transmission towers lost on the Planta Centro-Yaracuy line (600 MW lost from the national grid), power restored to 96% in La Guaira by 10 July; potable water restored to 84% by 10 July; the Port of La Guaira's container terminal suspended operations due to liquefaction-related damage; Simón Bolívar International Airport partially closed.

prevention.title: Prevention and mitigation
prevention.content: GEER documents Venezuela's 1982 seismic design code (COVENIN 1756-82), which specified a peak ground acceleration of 0.3g for Zone 4 (including Caracas and La Guaira) and required liquefaction assessment for loose sands within 20 m depth, indicating formal building-code provisions existed before the event. However, GEER's building-damage findings (severe damage/collapse of numerous residential and commercial structures in Playa Escondida, Caraballeda, Los Corales and Catia La Mar) and USGS PAGER's note that the population resides predominantly in unreinforced masonry and adobe structures indicate substantial gaps in code enforcement or retrofitting of older/informal building stock. Sediment-control dams built after the 1999 Vargas debris-flow disaster were in place along Cordillera de la Costa watersheds, though a 2005 inspection found 10 of 18 dams already mostly full of sediment with limited remaining storage capacity, suggesting pre-existing mitigation infrastructure had reduced capacity. No comprehensive land-use planning or retrofitting programme is described in the documents.

preparedness.title: Preparedness
preparedness.content: Venezuela maintains a national seismic network (FUNVISIS, 40 broadband stations) and a strong-motion network (REDAC, 134 accelerometers), though GEER notes that recorded waveforms from these networks were not made publicly available as of the report's publication, limiting situational awareness. National authorities declared a state of emergency and deployed search-and-rescue forces rapidly after the earthquake (25 June, ECHO Flash). Venezuela requested international assistance via the EU Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM) on 25 June, and seven countries offered assistance, indicating pre-existing international coordination channels. The documents do not describe specific public earthquake early-warning systems, drills, or stockpiles that were activated, representing a gap in reported preparedness information.

response.title: Response
response.content: National search-and-rescue operations began immediately on 24-25 June and continued for weeks, with over 6,460 people rescued by early July (UN OCHA/AVN). Venezuela requested UCPM assistance on 25 June, and the Copernicus Emergency Management Service was activated in rapid mapping mode (EMSR884) on 25 June, producing 33 maps covering 13 areas of interest by 20 July. The EU allocated EUR 5 million in emergency humanitarian aid funding (reported 30 June). By 21 July, UN OCHA counted 49 response organizations active (4 UN, 19 international, 25 national/local). International responders included the USS Fort Lauderdale (entering the Port of La Guaira from 28 June to support relief), International Medical Corps (mobile medical units, water trucking), IOM and UNICEF (together providing over 7,000 medical consultations and reaching over 20,000 people with primary health care and vaccination), PAHO/WHO-coordinated Emergency Medical Teams (14 operational by 23 July), WFP (reaching over 100,000 people with food assistance by late July via hot meals, ready-to-eat rations and dry food baskets), World Central Kitchen (over one million meals served by mid-July), IFRC (temporary health posts), and CISP (handwashing points). Constraints included damaged roads, debris, partial airport closure, and electrical/telecommunications failures that hampered coordination and family tracing, prompting use of satellite connectivity (Starlink) and assessment of repeater sites in Galipán. Commercial cargo was rerouted through Puerto Cabello, itself operating only partially due to insufficient power.

recovery.title: Recovery and reconstruction
recovery.content: Infrastructure restoration progressed over weeks: electricity in La Guaira reached 60% restoration by 27 June and 96% by 10 July (21 substations fully restored); potable water reached 84% restoration by 10 July, with the El Guapo Dam system in Barlovento (Miranda) reporting 83 of 91 pipeline failures repaired by 14 July and Páez and Andrés Bello municipalities fully restored, while Brión reached about 80% supply capacity. The El Palito refinery restarted its fluid catalytic cracker by 13 July; the Morón Petrochemical Complex restarted by 25 June. Port of La Guaira commercial operations were set to gradually resume from 21 July (per MAERSK); the affected airport runway was expected to allow resumed commercial operations from 24 August after resurfacing (teleSUR). The World Bank's GRADE assessment (USD 19.6 billion in direct physical damage) provides a basis for damage and loss quantification, though a detailed reconstruction plan or build-back-better framework is not described in the documents.

needs_gaps.title: Needs and gaps
needs_gaps.content: Shelter and protection needs were significant: UNHCR flagged that many temporary and improvised sites (churches, schools, stadiums) did not meet minimum standards for safety, privacy, lighting, water and sanitation, with rapid protection monitoring identifying risks to mental health, family separation, older persons, persons with disabilities and children. WASH needs were addressed partially: UNICEF provided about 80,000 litres of water per day via trucking and hygiene kits to 8,906 people, while IOM distributed over 1,500 collapsible water containers and 1,000 hygiene kits, but the scale of displacement (up to 1.3 million affected) suggests needs outpaced capacity. Health system needs included surge demand for orthopedic and neurosurgical care, damage to 38 hospitals, and the JRC health note's identified gaps in surveillance, continuity of maternal/neonatal and chronic-disease care, and immunisation coverage. The official number of missing people remained unknown for an extended period, with ECHO Flash noting on 29 June that approximately 46,000 people were still unaccounted for and media reporting around 43,000 missing as of 1 July, indicating a persistent information gap. GEER notes that FUNVISIS strong-motion waveform data were not publicly released, limiting independent engineering assessment.

lessons.title: Lessons and recommendations
lessons.content: The JRC health security note concludes that the best-supported, hazard-independent priorities are to sustain disease surveillance and early warning, protect and restore WASH and health infrastructure, maintain immunisation, ensure continuity of care, and provide mental health and psychosocial support, and that cross-border/inter-agency coordination (Health Cluster, EMT mechanisms, PAHO/WHO) should account for migration-linked disease spread. UNHCR and PAHO both document protection, shelter standards and food access as real health-security needs that should be planned explicitly rather than treated as secondary. GEER's geoscientific sections note that the 2026 event offers an unusually well-constrained opportunity to test geospatial liquefaction hazard models (e.g., Zhu et al. 2017) against field data, implying a recommendation to incorporate local in-situ testing into hazard modelling given the narrow, boulder-rich alluvial fans of the La Guaira coast that existing proxy-based models cannot resolve.

confidence.title: Information quality
confidence.content: Confidence is high for the ECHO Flash situation reports (24 June-21 July 2026) and GEER reconnaissance report (August 2026), which provide dated, source-attributed figures, though casualty, displacement and damage figures evolved substantially over time and sometimes differ between UN OCHA, AVN and later Venezuelan government/Reuters figures (e.g., 5,278 deaths per UN OCHA 20 July vs. over 6,000 deaths per Venezuelan government 3 August). The JRC health security note explicitly flags that casualty and damage figures for the 2026 earthquakes evolved and differ between PAHO and UNHCR, and that national disease-burden figures carry surveillance-related uncertainty. Economic loss estimates vary by methodology and date (GEM: USD 4.1-7.9 billion; World Bank GRADE: USD 19.6 billion). Information gaps include unreleased FUNVISIS instrumental waveform data, an unresolved final missing-persons count, and limited detail in the documents on formal preparedness systems (early warning, drills, stockpiles) prior to the event.

passages.text: VENEZUELA Health Security Aspects Health security risks arising from chronic health-system fragility and recurrent natural-hazard emergencies USGS Macroseismic Intensity (ShakeMap) for the M7.2 earthquake, 21 km ENE of San Felipe, Venezuela, 24 June 2026. Source: U.S. Geological Survey (public domain). Prepared by: Sandra COECKE F7 - ETOHA EMBRACE project team This document draws on the JRC Hurricane Beryl emergency report (JRC138792), peer-reviewed and grey literature on Venezuela, and the latest PAHO/WHO and UNHCR reporting on the 24 June 2026 earthquakes. All figures are attributed to their source and reporting date; none have been invented. Executive summary Health security in Venezuela is shaped less by any single hazard than by the interaction between a chronically weakened health system and recurrent acute emergencies. The country enters each crisis with pre-existing socio-economic and humanitarian vulnerabilities: millions of people already face difficulties accessing health care, safe water, food and other basic services, which raises vulnerability to the health impacts of emergencies and disasters (PAHO/WHO, Public Health Situation Analysis, 10 July 2026). Two recent events illustrate how hazards translate into health consequences. Hurricane Beryl (July 2024), the earliest Category 5 Atlantic hurricane on record, caused flooding and casualties in north-eastern Venezuela, with the waterborne and vector-borne disease risks typical of post-hurricane settings. The 24 June 2026 earthquakes (M7.2 and M7.5) in north-central Venezuela caused mass casualties, displacement and damage to health facilities, producing an acute public health emergency on top of the structural crisis. Across these events the pattern is consistent: damage to water, sanitation and health infrastructure; elevated risk of vaccine-preventable, vector-borne and waterborne disease; disruption to continuity of care for chronic conditions and for maternal and neonatal health; and a heavy mental health and psychosocial burden.

The priorities that hold regardless of the hazard are to strengthen disease surveillance, protect WASH and health-facility capacity, sustain immunisation, and provide mental health and psychosocial support. 1. Baseline: chronic health-system fragility Health security in Venezuela cannot be assessed without the structural baseline. The literature documents a sustained deterioration of the public health system since the mid-2010s, with the re-emergence of previously controlled or eliminated infectious diseases following the economic and health-system crisis (Paniz-Mondolfi et al., Emerging Infectious Diseases, 2019; ECDC rapid risk assessment, 2019). Re-emergence of vaccine-preventable diseases (measles, diphtheria) and vector-borne diseases, reported as a regional public-health threat for the Americas because of cross-border spread.

passages.text: Beryl affected several Caribbean countries and caused flooding and casualties in north-eastern Venezuela (including the Sucre area), with deaths and missing persons reported. The JRC emergency report (JRC138792) and its open-source health monitoring identify the post-hurricane health risks relevant to flood-affected communities: Waterborne disease from contaminated drinking water: cholera, dysentery, leptospirosis, hepatitis A, typhoid and gastrointestinal illness. Vector-borne disease from standing water: dengue, Zika, chikungunya and malaria. Injuries, including puncture wounds and tetanus risk from contaminated flood water. Mental health impacts (anxiety, depression, PTSD) after loss of homes and livelihoods. Malnutrition and dehydration risk for vulnerable groups where infrastructure is lost. The report also highlights wastewater surveillance as an early-warning tool for waterborne pathogens, where infrastructure allows. The 24 June 2026 earthquakes (M7.2 and M7.5) Two consecutive earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela, affecting at least seven states, with La Guaira and the Greater Caracas area most severely impacted; hundreds to over a thousand aftershocks followed in the following weeks. The health consequences reported by PAHO/WHO and UNHCR are: Mass trauma casualties and surgical demand (orthopedics, neurosurgery), with hospitals operating under extreme pressure. Damage to health facilities and to water, sanitation, power, telecommunications and transport infrastructure. Outbreak risk among displaced and overcrowded populations: vaccine-preventable disease (measles, diphtheria, pertussis), yellow fever, and vector-borne disease (dengue, chikungunya, Zika, Oropouche, malaria), several already circulating. Disruption to continuity of care, notably maternal and neonatal care, and exacerbation of malnutrition. A heavy mental health and psychosocial burden, and protection risks in substandard temporary shelters.

passages.text: Mental health and psychosocial support (Psychological First Aid, standardized protocols, training of frontline workers) is an integral, ongoing component of the response. UNHCR adds the protection and shelter dimension: many temporary and improvised sites (churches, schools, stadiums) did not yet meet minimum standards for safety, privacy, lighting, water and sanitation, with rapid protection monitoring flagging mental health, family separation and risks to older persons, persons with disabilities and children. 4. Recurring health-security risk nodes Across both the hurricane and the earthquake emergencies, the same risk nodes recur. The table summarises each node, the main drivers observed in Venezuela, and the groups most exposed. Risk node Main drivers in Venezuela Most exposed Health-system capacity Facility damage, power/cold-chain gaps, workforce shortages, surge demand. Whole population; trauma and emergency patients. Waterborne disease WASH disruption, contaminated water, flooding, crowded shelters. Children, displaced and shelter populations. Vector-borne disease Standing water, weakened vector control; dengue, malaria and others already circulating. Coastal and peri-urban communities. Vaccine-preventable disease Low baseline coverage, surveillance gaps, population movement (measles, diphtheria, pertussis, yellow fever). Unvaccinated children; displaced groups. Continuity of care Disruption to maternal/neonatal care, chronic-disease treatment and rehabilitation. Pregnant women, newborns, people with chronic conditions. Nutrition Supply disruption, displacement, loss of food access. Children, pregnant women, the elderly. Mental health Trauma, loss, displacement, overwhelmed services. Affected communities, families of the missing, responders. 5. Governance and response priorities The measures below strengthen the underlying system and pay off regardless of which hazard comes next. They mirror the priorities PAHO/WHO and partners are already pursuing. Sustain disease surveillance and early warning. Maintain a priority notifiable-disease list, integrate surveillance with infection prevention and control in shelters, and use tools such as wastewater surveillance and open-source epidemic intelligence for early detection. Protect and restore WASH and health infrastructure.

passages.pdf_filename: Venezuela_Health_Security_Aspects_clean.docx
passages.text: Mental health and psychosocial support. Provide Psychological First Aid, standardized protocols and training for frontline workers, targeting affected communities, families of the missing and responders. Cross-border and inter-agency coordination. Coordinate through the Health Cluster, EMT mechanisms and regional bodies (PAHO/WHO), and account for cross-border disease spread linked to migration. Protection and shelter standards and food access are not purely clinical measures, but UNHCR and PAHO both document them as real health-security needs; they should be planned explicitly. 6. Strength of evidence and limitations Casualty and damage figures for the 2026 earthquakes evolved across reports and differ between PAHO and UNHCR; reporting dates are given throughout and figures should be read as point-in-time, not final. The Beryl report quantifies regional exposure but notes that flood figures for Venezuela were limited by observation and data resolution; health impacts there are described qualitatively. Baseline disease burden (malaria, measles, diphtheria) is well documented in peer-reviewed and grey literature, but surveillance gaps mean national figures are uncertain. Scientific field-mission reporting on the 2026 earthquakes (EDCMS Newsletter No.32, Lekkas, Carydis, Mavroulis et al., NKUA, July 2026) provides geoscientific and disaster-management context; this document defers to PAHO/WHO for health-specific figures. The best-supported conclusions are the system-level measures (surveillance, WASH, immunisation, continuity of care, mental health). Hazard-specific numbers rest on thinner or evolving evidence. passages.text: Venezuela - Earthquakes. Two strong earthquakes struck north-western Venezuela. The first event, with a magnitude of 7.2 M, occurred on 24 June at 22:04 UTC (18:04 local time) at a depth of 20 km. Its epicentre was located 23 km south-east of Yumare town (Yaracuy State) and 170 km south of the capital, Caracas. The second event, with a magnitude of 7.5 M, occurred one minute later at a depth of 10 km; its epicentre was located 28 km south-east of Yumare. USGS PAGER estimates that, combining the two earthquakes, approximately 37 000 people were exposed to violent shaking, 347 000 to severe shaking, 627 000 to very strong shaking, and 6 993 000 to strong shaking. According to initial reports, at least 32 people have died, and at least 700 others have been injured. Several buildings collapsed, particularly in parts of Caracas and in nearby towns. National authorities have declared a state of emergency and deployed search and rescue forces to locate people trapped under the rubble of collapsed buildings. On 25 June, the Copernicus Emergency Management Service (EMS) was activated in rapid mapping mode ( EMSR884 ) to support damage assessment.

The humanitarian impact of the two strong earthquakes (7.2 and 7.5 M, respectively) that occurred in the state of Yaracuy in north-western Venezuela on 24 June is increasing. La Guaira state is the most affected, with Falcón, Yaracuy, Carabobo, Aragua, Miranda states and the capital district of Caracas. As of 26 June, media reports at least 235 fatalities and 4 300 injured people across the affected states. Approximately 46 000 people are still unaccounted for, with at least 200 people still trapped under rubble, and more than 70 000 people have been affected only in La Guaira state. More than 250 buildings were destroyed or damaged, the Caracas main airport was closed, and power outages were reported in several areas. National authorities declared a state of emergency, search and rescue operation is still ongoing. On 25 June, Venezuela requested assistance from the Union Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), and seven countries offered assistance. On the same date, the Copernicus Emergency Management Service (EMS) was activated in rapid mapping mode (EMSR884) to support damage assessment. One map has been produced so far.

passages.text: June 24, 2026, San Felipe and Catia La Mar Earthquakes 104 August 2026 4. GEOLOGIC SETTING Table 4-1. Main Authors of this Section Name Affiliation Eduardo Carrillo Professional, Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. 4.1 Summary The June 24th 2026 earthquakes severely affected two densely populated sectors of central Venezuela: La Guaira State and the Caracas Valley. Both areas are located along the tectonically active Cordillera de la Costa and are underlain by complex metamorphic bedrock overlain by heterogeneous Quaternary deposits. In La Guaira, damage was concentrated in coastal settlements developed on Holocene alluvial fans and marine terraces. These deposits, locally exceeding 400 m in thickness, record the combined influence of high-gradient mountain drainage, coastal processes, debris-flow sedimentation, and active deformation associated with regional structures such as the San Sebastián Fault system. The presence of thick, unconsolidated fan deposits and potentially liquefaction-prone coastal and lagoonal sediments likely contributed to variable seismic ground response and localized damage patterns. In the Caracas Valley, earthquake impacts were primarily associated with areas underlain by thick and laterally variable Quaternary basin-fill deposits, including alluvial, colluvial, lacustrine, and debris-flow sediments. The distribution and thickness of these deposits are strongly controlled by fault-related uplift, subsidence, drainage obstruction, and repeated mass-transport processes linked to the Tacagua-El Ávila structural system. This stratigraphic complexity produces significant contrasts in stiffness, compressibility, groundwater conditions, and seismic-wave propagation characteristics, which are critical factors for evaluating seismic site effects and geotechnical performance. Overall, the geological framework of La Guaira and Caracas indicates that earthquake damage patterns are closely related to the interaction between active tectonics, steep geomorphology, thick unconsolidated Quaternary deposits, and recurrent debris-flow processes.

passages.text: June 24, 2026, San Felipe and Catia La Mar Earthquakes 110 August 2026 5. SEISMICITY AND EARTHQUAKE-SOURCE CHARACTERISTICS Table 5-1. Main Authors of this Section Name Affiliation Shiying Nie Senior Earthquake Scientist at Karen Clark & Company, USA 5.1 Summary Northern Venezuela lies within a broad transpressional plate-boundary zone between the Caribbean and South American plates. The principal dextral structure is the Boconó–San Sebastián–El Pilar fault system; the Oca-Ancón system is an important secondary dextral system in northwestern Venezuela (Audemard et al., 2000, 2006). The first subevent (M7.2) originated in the western source region, where the regional fault map shows the northeast-striking Boconó system approaching the approximately east–west San Sebastián system (Figure 1-2). The strand that hosted the initial subevent and the transfer geometry remains uncertain (USGS, 2026a, 2026b). The June 24, 2026, Venezuela earthquakes were two large strike-slip subevents separated by approximately 29.6 seconds in the current USGS catalog and 33.2 seconds in the GFZ/GEOFON catalog. Current USGS and GFZ moment tensor solutions place the first origin in the western source region and the M7.5 hypocenter offshore La Guaira, near Catia La Mar. The USGS finitefault solution represents sequence-related slip on two steeply dipping segments using seismic, InSAR, and GNSS constraints. The spatial sequence and rapid source information are broadly consistent with west-to-east source progression, although rupture speed and the transfer path remain uncertain. Possible transition paths include transfer between the Boconó and San Sebastián fault systems and participation of parallel or branching strands. Optical image correlation identifies possible tectonic near-surface deformation at La Guaira, while the Caraballeda signal is more consistent with lateral spreading or gravitational sliding. Eastward progression makes directivity plausible, but source proximity and Caracas basin response also require evaluation.

This section summarizes the seismic networks with potential or available records for these events and describes how more distant waveform data were identified and compiled for subsequent processing. Because near-source instrumental data remain limited, indirect observations such as reported shaking intensity and USGS ShakeMap products are also used to provide broader context for the spatial distribution and severity of ground shaking. 6.2.1 Seismic Networks in the Region 6.2.1.1 FUNVISIS network Venezuela has a national seismic network (FDSN code: VE) operated by FUNVISIS. This network consists of 40 stations equipped with broadband seismometers (Güralp CMG-40T-1) distributed across the country's higher-seismicity zones (Figure 6-17). Additionally, FUNVISIS operates a strong ground motion network (Red Acelerogáfica Nacional, REDAC) comprising 134 accelerometers (Kinemetrics Etna) installed across the country’s main urban centers (Figure 6-18) (FUNVISIS, 2023). Although the number of operational stations in both networks is unclear, there is evidence that some of these stations (e.g., CARV, FUNV, BENV in Figure 6-17) were in operation during the San Felipe and Catia La Mar June 2026 earthquakes. However, as of the publication of this report, the recorded waveforms were not publicly available.

Main Authors of this Section Name Affiliation Patricia Varela Senior Geologist, Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. 7.1 Summary Earthquake-induced ground deformation has been reported across multiple regions of northern Venezuela following the June 2026 earthquakes, including observations of ground cracking, liquefaction, landslides, and damage to infrastructure. However, the highest concentration of reported impacts occurred within the Caracas Metropolitan Area and the neighboring state of La Guaira (formerly Vargas), where population density, infrastructure exposure, and the severity of observed ground effects were the greatest. Accordingly, the remote reconnaissance effort focused on these areas by defining an area of interest encompassing the most heavily affected portions of Caracas and La Guaira. This targeted approach allowed for a systematic review of post-earthquake aerial and satellite imagery to identify, map, and classify potential earthquake-induced ground deformation features and support subsequent field verification activities. A remote geomorphic assessment was conducted using pre- and post-earthquake aerial imagery to identify ground deformation features attributable to the June 2026 earthquakes. The analysis consisted of systematic visual comparisons between pre- and post-event imagery to identify geomorphic changes that were absent in pre-earthquake conditions. 7.2 Ground Deformation Inventory Features identified during the review were compiled into a geospatial inventory and classified according to the criteria described below. This dataset is available on DesignSafe.  Ground Rupture  Fracture – Ground cracks exhibiting no visible displacement and no evidence of liquefaction-triggering related processes.  Fault – Ground cracks displaying observable vertical or horizontal displacement indicative of surface fault rupture.

The original debris flow hazard maps were developed under Proyecto Ávila (IMF-UCV, 2002). Figure shows the high-debris flow hazard map; it does not include medium- or low-hazard areas. For Mamo, La Zorra, Tacagua, Piedra Azul, Alcantarilla, San José de Galipán (Macuto), Quebrada Seca, and Cerro Grande coastal watersheds, updated debris flow hazard maps incorporating the influence of sediment-control dams were used (Courtel et al., 2021). 10.4 Compounding Hazards Debris flow and flash flood events along the Cordillera de la Costa north of Caracas are recurrent hazards rather than isolated events, with historical events documented in 1798, 1938, 1948, and 1951 (Altez, 2005). The impacts from these events, however, are difficult to directly compare with that of 1999 given changes in population density and urban development (Altez & Urbani, 2021). The first significant storm that tested the performance of the sediment-control dams built in response to the 1999 event took place in February 2005. It delivered 431 mm of rainfall (as measured at the Macuto hydrometeorological station) along the Cordillera de la Costa and caused debris flow and flash floods that impacted many of the same areas impacted in 1999 (Lopez, 2020). The 2005 event was important in remobilizing sediment that had accumulated but was not transported to the sea in 1999, with a total volume of deposited sediment of 800,000 m3 (Lopez, 2020). An inspection of the sediment-control dams carried out by FUNVISIS and the Institute of Fluid Mechanics of the Central University of Venezuela (FUNVISIS & IMF-UCV, 2005) after the 2005 event indicated that out of 18 inspected dams, 10 were mostly full of sediment but still with some capacity left for additional storage.

The observed damage includes distress and collapse of wall and façade elements, as well as more substantial damage to portions of individual structures.

passages.text: June 24 2026 San Felipe and Catia La Mar Earthquakes i August, 2026 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY On June 24, 2026, two earthquakes affected northern Venezuela within approximately 30 seconds of one another: an M7.2 event near San Felipe, Yaracuy, followed by an M7.5 event offshore La Guaira near Catia La Mar. The sequence occurred within the broad transpressional plate-boundary zone between the Caribbean and South American plates, where right-lateral motion is distributed across the Boconó–San Sebastián–El Pilar and related fault systems. The earthquakes produced severe and spatially variable impacts across the north-central region of the country, with the most significant damage concentrated in La Guaira, particularly Catia La Mar, Caraballeda, Macuto, Maiquetía, and neighboring coastal communities, as well as localized but notable impacts in Caracas, including San Bernardino and Los Palos Grandes. The events caused major loss of life, widespread damage to buildings and infrastructure, displacement of residents, disruption to essential services, and direct physical losses estimated in the tens of billions of U.S. dollars. dollars. The GEER Association organized a rapid hybrid reconnaissance effort to document the geotechnical, geological, seismological, and infrastructure-related effects of these earthquakes. The reconnaissance combined remote data collection, satellite and aerial imagery review, social media and news media georeferencing, collaboration with local professionals and students, field visits, drone surveys, limited subsurface investigation, and coordination with national and international organizations. The GEER team worked closely with Venezuelan academic institutions, the Venezuelan Society of Geotechnical Engineering, local engineering practitioners, students, government agencies, and international organizations to collect and preserve perishable data before cleanup, demolition, rainfall, and emergency response activities altered the evidence. This report provides a coordinated, source-documented record of early observations and identifies priority needs for future investigation. The M7.5 rupture was located close to the densely populated coastal corridor of La Guaira, and the sequence appears to have involved west-to-east rupture progression along strike-slip fault segments.

A large oil leak was reported at the El Palito Refinery, the country’s smallest refinery, following the earthquake (Figure 13-1).14 The refinery’s operations were interrupted due to a loss of electrical power from damaged transmission lines supplying the facility.15 As of 13 July 2026, El Palito restarted its fluid catalytic cracker, with other operational units reactivated slowly.16 The nearby Morón Petrochemical Complex, Venezuela’s second largest petrochemical complex, sustained damage, including collapsed storage infrastructure and a storage tank leak. Operations at the facility were temporarily suspended while damage assessments and safety inspections were conducted before the complex was restarted on Thursday, 25 June. 17 Despite these localized disruptions, Venezuela's main oil output regions such as the Orinoco Belt and in Western Venezuela continued operating without significant damage or production interruptions.

The Planta Centro Power Station, operated by CORPOELEC, experienced a temporary shutdown following the earthquake but was successfully restarted by June 25 after inspections and restoration of supporting infrastructure.23 Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, stated that there had been power outages in Caracas and La Guaira,24 and there were reports of lost cellphone service in parts of Caracas.25 There were additional reports of loss of power across numerous states immediately following the earthquake, including Barquisimeto, Coro, Maracay, Mérida, Nueva Esparta, San Cristóbal, and Valencia.26 In several locations these outages compounded existing reliability issues within the Venezuelan electrical grid,27 making it difficult to distinguish earthquake-induced failures from chronic service interruptions. Restoration efforts progressed during the days following the earthquake. By June 27, approximately 60% of electrical service had reportedly been restored in La Guaira.28,29 By July 10, restoration of electrical services increased to 96% with 21 electrical substations fully restored.30 Continued restoration depended upon repairs to a damaged transmission tower located within the mountainous terrain of the state, illustrating the importance of transmission infrastructure in reestablishing regional power service. passages.text: 13.3 Water and Wastewater Initial Impacts Water service disruptions were reported across multiple regions following the earthquake. Residents of Caracas reported interruptions to potable water service beginning shortly after the event,31 while damage to buried water infrastructure resulted in burst water mains that caused localized street flooding in western portions of the city.32 Additional water service disruptions were reported in parts of Caracas, Miranda, Falcón, Yaracuy, Zulia, and La Guaira, suggesting that impacts extended beyond the immediate area of strongest shaking.33 Reported disruptions were likely attributable to a combination of pipeline damage, power outages affecting pumping facilities, and precautionary shutdowns while utilities assessed system integrity. Recovery of potable water services reached 84% by July 10, 2026, as reported by the acting president.34 The El Guapo Dam distribution system (which supplies the municipalities of Pedro Gual, Páez, Andrés Bello, Eulalia Buroz, and Brión in the Barlovento sub-region of Miranda State) sustained a total of 91 failures along approximately 75 km of water mains following the June 24 earthquakes. As of July 14, 2026, 83 of these 91 failures (91%) had already been repaired through a coordinated response involving local municipalities, and the municipalities of Páez and Andrés Bello had water services fully restored. The Brión municipality had recovered to approximately 80% of its supply capacity as of July 14, 2026. On the same day, repair crews were continuing work on a pipeline fracture between the La Gran Parada and Los Canales sectors in Páez municipality (Figure 13-2), which had affected seven communities (El Jobo, El Parral, Cangrejal, El Crucero, Los Canales, Las Flores, and Catia).35 31 Caliber. passages.text: Commercial operations are expected to resume gradually from Aug. 24 after resurfacing work is completed on runway (teleSUR; last accessed July 30th 2026).36 Maritime transportation also experienced major disruptions. The Port of La Guaira, located near the area of strongest shaking, suspended commercial operations due to structural damage of the Container Terminal (CMA CGM, 2026). Liquefaction-triggering effects (e.g., lateral spreading) were documented at the port and are believed to have contributed to the observed damage. Emergency supply vessels including the USS Fort Lauderdale were able to enter the port as early as June 28 to support disaster-relief and humanitarian assistance efforts (US Southern Command, 2026). In the weeks following the earthquakes, the port has served as a disaster recovery hub, as well as a temporary morgue for victims. Commercial cargo was rerouted through Puerto Cabello. As of June 26, Puerto Cabello was operating only partially because of insufficient electrical power, reducing the capacity available to absorb diverted maritime traffic and potentially affecting regional supply chains. Commercial operations are set to gradually resume at the Port of La Guaira as of July 21st (MAERSK, 2026) Within Caracas, public transportation services were temporarily suspended to facilitate emergency response and recovery operations. Subway and rail systems were shut down while inspections were conducted and rescue activities proceeded, limiting mobility throughout the metropolitan area during the immediate aftermath of the earthquake. Ground transportation was also affected by restrictions on the primary highway connecting La Guaira and Caracas. Access along this critical transportation corridor was limited, with roadway use reserved primarily for emergency response personnel during the initial response period. These restrictions constrained movement between the capital and Venezuela's principal international airport and nearby coastal communities. Reconnaissance Findings from GEER field team Reconnaissance observations indicated that transportation infrastructure sustained both structural and geotechnical damage, with the most severe impacts concentrated in coastal communities. The Catia La Mar bus terminal exhibited widespread structural failure in beams and connections, as well as widespread masonry collapse and slab breakage associated with a flexible diaphragm response. One of the products issued is the Prompt Assessment of Global Earthquakes for Response (PAGER), an automated system that uses seismic data from remote sensors to rapidly estimate the shaking intensity and the extent of the impacts of earthquakes globally (USGS 2026). For the M7.5 earthquake, the USGS initially estimated its epicenter to be 20 km ESE of Yumare. Based on this understanding, PAGER issued a red alert for human and economic losses, indicating that high casualty figures and extensive damage were likely and that the disaster would be widespread. The model estimated that economic losses could amount to approximately 5% to 20% of Venezuela’s GDP, and noted that the population in the region resides primarily in vulnerable structures, predominantly unreinforced masonry buildings and adobe blocks.

INTRODUCTION On June 24, 2026, while Venezuela was on a statutory Federal holiday, at 18:04:31 local time (22:04:31 Coordinated Universal Time [UTC]) a moment magnitude, M, 7.2 earthquake occurred with its epicenter near the city of San Felipe, in the State of Yaracuy, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS). This earthquake had an epicenter located at 10.622, −67.194 km ENE of Catia La Mar, in the State of La Guaira (see Figure 1-1). The hypocentral depth of this earthquake was 10 km (USGS 2026b). passages.text: June 24, 2026, San Felipe and Catia La Mar Earthquakes 34 August 2026 As shown in Figure 1-2 and Figure 1-3, Northern Venezuela is located within a broad transpressional plate-boundary zone between the Caribbean and South American plates. Rightlateral plate motion is distributed among several active faults, principally the Boconó-San Sebastián-El Pilar and Oca-Ancón systems (Audemard 2000). Figure 1-2. Diagram of Plate Boundaries for Venezuela (modified from Audemard 2000). The M7.5 event occurred as a result of shallow strike-slip faulting near the Caribbean and South America plate boundary (USGS; last accessed August 2, 2026). As seen in Figure 1-2, the Caribbean plate is moving eastward relative to the South America plate at an approximate rate of 18-20 millimeters per year (mm/yr). The USGS finite rupture model developed for the M7.5 event indicates a length of rupture of about 175 km and a width of approximately 20 km. The Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences reported two sub-ruptures of M7.3 (at the northeastern end of the Boconó Fault) and M7.4 (along the right-lateral San Sebastián Fault). The latter trends east-west (as seen in Figure 1-2 and Figure 1-3) and is located 10 to 15 km north of Caracas, Venezuela’s capital. The epicenter of these earthquakes were within 250 km of the most populated area of the country including the capital, Caracas, with a population of about 5.5 million, and Valencia and Maracay, which are the third and fifth largest cities in the country (see Figure 1-4). News reports immediately following the seismic events indicated significant damage to structures located to the east and south of the first and second epicenters, respectively. The June 24, 2026 earthquakes caused over 6,000 deaths, and injured nearly 61,000 people according to official figures released by the Venezuelan government on August 3, 2026 (Reuters1). The earthquakes also generated $19.6 billion USD in direct physical damage according to the World Bank Group and based on the Global Rapid Damage Estimation (GRADE) methodology. 1 https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/death-toll-venezuela-june-earthquakes-tops-6000-2026-08-03/

Initially, the GEER remote team collected, curated, and validated useful information from the post-disaster coverage and immediate disaster social media reports. Concurrently, the GEER team, drawing on its strong connections in Venezuela and abroad, collaborated with local academics, engineers and students already near the affected areas to collect additional high-quality data on the geotechnical consequences identified by the remote team. The GEER team co-leaders also participated in three response coordination meetings led by the Earthquake Engineering Research Institute (EERI) Learning from Earthquakes (LFE) Program’s chairs (i.e., Robb Moss and Ayse Hortacsu), where helpful context was provided and local professionals and international interested groups were in attendance. Main Authors of this Section Name Affiliation Eduardo Carrillo Professional, Geosyntec Consultants, USA 3.1 Summary The June 24th 2026 earthquakes in northern Venezuela occurred within the complex Caribbean– South America plate boundary, where deformation is accommodated by the North Andean Block and distributed across major dextral transpressional fault systems (Audemard, 2002). The sequence is interpreted to have initiated along the Boconó Fault System with an M 7.2 event and subsequently propagated northeastward onto the San Sebastián Fault, where a larger M 7.5 earthquake produced severe impacts along the north-central Venezuelan coast and the Metropolitan Area. Geological, geodetic, and seismotectonic evidence indicate that the Boconó– San Sebastián–El Pilar fault system concentrates much of the relative motion between the Caribbean Plate, the Maracaibo and Bonaire blocks, and stable South America. Historical earthquakes, including the destructive 1812, 1900, and 1967 events, together with paleoseismic investigations along the Boconó Fault, demonstrate that this plate-boundary system has generated recurrent large-magnitude earthquakes over centennial to millennial timescales (Pousse-Beltran et al., 2017: Perez et al., 2018; Audemard et al., 2000; Audemard, 2002; and Hernandez and Schmitz, 2023. The apparent spatial overlap between the 1812 and 2026 ruptures suggests that the 2026 M7.2 and M7.5 events may represent a recurrent earthquake cycle affecting the Caracas–La Guaira area. These findings emphasize the seismic hazard posed by active strike-slip and transpressional faults in northern Venezuela, particularly where fault rupture, basin amplification, and dense urban development interact to increase earthquake risk.

node_types.hazard: A physical event or process that can cause harm, including the main earthquake shock, aftershocks/foreshocks, and secondary/cascading hazards such as landslides, liquefaction, tsunami, dam failure, fire or technological accidents.
node_types.impact: A concrete effect of a hazard or vulnerability on people, assets, services, the economy or the environment, including deaths, damage to buildings and infrastructure, displacement, service disruption, social/security effects and economic losses.
node_types.vulnerability: A pre-existing physical, social, environmental or systemic condition that increases susceptibility to harm from hazards, such as unreinforced structures, poverty, exposure factors or infrastructure fragility.
node_types.measure: An action, plan, system, policy, technology or capacity - spanning prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery - that prevents, mitigates, or addresses hazards, impacts, vulnerabilities or needs.
node_types.need: An unmet requirement or gap reported in the documents, ranging from life-saving needs to basic needs, services/access needs, protection and information needs.
node_types.actor: An organisation, institution or group that acts before, during or after an earthquake, including authorities, humanitarian organisations, scientific/monitoring bodies, research institutions and affected communities.

prevents.definition: A measure stops the target from happening at all (or would have, if recommended/lacking).

mitigates.definition: A measure reduces the severity or extent of the target.

triggers.definition: A hazard sets off another (cascading) hazard.

amplifies.definition: A vulnerability or impact makes the target worse without causing it alone.

addresses.definition: A measure responds to a need.

implements.definition: An actor carries out or provides a measure.

informs.definition: An actor or a measure (e.g. monitoring, modelling, reconnaissance, rapid mapping) produces information/data that supports or guides another measure.

exacerbates.definition: A vulnerability increases the likelihood or severity of another vulnerability or of a hazard occurring/worsening.

coordinates_with.definition: An actor coordinates or collaborates with another actor in planning, response or research activities.
